Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify variables associated with femoral shaft fractures that warrant additional evaluation (ie,
nonaccidental trauma, neurovascular injury).
Choose a fixation method for the management of pediatric femoral shaft fractures based on
patient age, patient weight, fracture pattern, and additional contributing factors.
Use surgical techniques designed to minimize the risk of described complications.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Diaphyseal femur fractures are commonly encountered in pediatric orthopaedic settings.
Appropriate treatment plans incorporate several clinical and sociodemographic factors.


Overview
Historically, traction and cast immobilization were standard in young children with a
femoral shaft fracture; however, longer durations of immobilization and hospital length
of stay, early disability, and the burden of home care associated with nonsurgical
management have shifted treatment algorithms to favor surgical stabilization for school-
aged children. In selecting an appropriate treatment plan, several patient and surgeon
factors must be considered. Considerable overlap exists among age-directed treatment
options. High-quality evidence that may help minimize this overlap is surprisingly limited.
The 2020 American Academy of Orthopedic Surgeons Evidence-Based Clinical Practice
Guideline on the Treatment of Pediatric Diaphyseal Femur Fractures cited strong or
moderate evidence for three of seven recommendations regarding pediatric femur
fractures1 (Table 1). Regardless, a general treatment algorithm has been agreed on via
expert consensus.2

Epidemiology/Etiology (Mechanism of Injury)
Most femoral fractures in children are caused by accidental trauma.

However, children younger than 3 years with a diaphyseal femur fracture should be evaluated
for possible child abuse.
In younger children, femoral fractures are most likely the result of a fall, whereas in older
children, motor vehicle collisions are a more common cause. The mechanism and energy of
the trauma determine the complexity of the fracture pattern.
Pathologic fractures also occur in children with local pathology (eg, bone cyst, benign or
malignant tumors) or systemic conditions (eg, osteogenesis imperfecta, cerebral palsy,
myelomeningocele).

Epidemiology/Etiology (Mechanism of Injury)
In pediatric patients, the estimated annual incidence of diaphyseal femur fractures is 19
per 100,000.3 Diaphyseal femur fractures account for 1.4% to 1.7% of all pediatric
fractures.4,5 The most common mechanism of injury differs by age group and
sociodemographic factors. In young children (<6 years), femoral shaft fractures most
frequently occur during a fall, whereas in older children (≥6 years), femoral shaft
fractures are associated with high-energy mechanisms of injury (motor vehicle‒
pedestrian accidents or motor vehicle accidents).3
These age-related mechanisms of injury are associated with a few exceptions. Strong
evidence suggests that children younger than 3 years with a diaphyseal femur fracture
should be evaluated for child abuse3,6,7 The incidence of child abuse associated with a
diaphyseal femur fracture in this age group is approximately 12% to 14%, and it
decreases substantially in older children. Evaluation should consist of a detailed patient
history, clinical survey for additional injuries, and input from additional personnel
involved in the child’s care. Providers should suspect nonaccidental trauma if a confusing
patient history is provided, the timing of care is inappropriate, and/or additional injuries
are present8 (Resource 1). A skeletal survey and consultation with an institution-specific
child abuse team should occur if deemed appropriate by the treating physician.
Children with neuromuscular disease (ie, cerebral palsy, myelomeningocele) often
sustain a femoral fracture during a low-energy mechanism of injury because of
osteopenia. This demographic also is at risk for child abuse. In addition, a common

diagnostic dilemma occurs if an insensate patient with myelomeningocele presents with
a swollen, erythematous, potentially healing femoral fracture; infection should be
included in the differential diagnosis for such patients.
Radiographs should be scrutinized for underlying pathologic femoral lesions (eg,
nonossifying fibroma, unicameral or aneurysmal bone cyst), especially if the mechanism
of injury in an older child is a low-energy mechanism.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
Femoral growth and morphology are directed by the proximal/distal femoral physes and the
greater/lesser trochanteric apophyses.
Vascular Anatomy
A tenuous blood supply to the femoral head (via branches of the medial femoral circumflex
artery) precludes safe entry into the proximal femur intramedullary canal via the piriformis
fossa because of the risk of femoral head osteonecrosis (Figure 1).

Deforming Forces
Femoral shaft fractures displace in a predictable pattern according to their location and
associated muscular attachments (Figure 2).


Anatomy and Biomechanics
In children with a femoral shaft fracture, the morphology of the proximal and distal
femur plays a role in remodeling potential and extra-physeal fixation options. The distal
femoral physis consists of undulations below a fan-shaped metaphysis and is
responsible for 70% of total femoral growth. The proximal femoral shaft is primarily
bound by the proximal femoral physis (responsible for approximately 30% of total
femoral length), femoral neck, greater trochanteric apophysis (involved in appositional
growth of the proximal femur), and intertrochanteric region. The greater trochanteric
apophysis contributes to clinically meaningful appositional growth until approximately a
child is aged 8 to 9 years. In patients younger than 8 years, disruption of the greater
trochanteric apophysis may lead to femoral neck narrowing and coxa valga. A tenuous
blood supply to the femoral head via retinacular vessels precludes safe entry into the
femoral intramedullary canal via the piriformis fossa. Therefore, lateral, trochanteric
entry, locked intramedullary nails have been designed for use in older children.
Injury Classification
Femoral fractures are described according to their location (proximal, middle, distal) and
fracture pattern (transverse, oblique, comminuted).
In older children, optimal fixation options also are classified as length stable (transverse, short
oblique) versus length unstable (long oblique, comminuted).

Injury Classification
Femoral shaft fractures typically are described by referencing the location (eg,
subtrochanteric/proximal, middle, distal) and the fracture pattern (via descriptive
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Femoral Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001058
8/31

nomenclature such as transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted). Open fractures are
classified according to the Gustilo and Anderson classification system.
In selecting a fixation strategy for older children, fractures are further classified as length
stable or length unstable. Typically, transverse and short oblique fractures are
considered stable, whereas spiral/long oblique and comminuted fractures are
considered unstable. Authors variably define short (or long) as less than (or greater than)
one9 versus two10 cortical diameters at the fracture site.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient history, physical examination, and plain radiographs usually are sufficient to guide the
management of pediatric femur fractures.
Hemodynamic instability or declining hematocrit/hemoglobin levels should not be attributed
to an isolated pediatric femoral shaft fracture.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
If a femoral fracture is known or suspected, a detailed patient history, physical
examination, and orthopedic trauma imaging studies should be obtained. In children
younger than 3 years, nonaccidental trauma should be considered, and the patient
history should be scrutinized for rationality. Despite recent trends toward surgical
management, isolated pediatric femoral shaft fractures are not associated with
hemodynamic instability or declining hematocrit/hemoglobin levels. With such fractures,
additional injuries or sources of blood loss should be suspected11-13 (Resource 2).
Orthogonal plain radiographs of the femur usually are diagnostic. In young children,
initial radiographs may forecast shortening in a cast but not necessarily angulation after
closed reduction. Advanced imaging studies are considered only in special scenarios. The
incidence of associated femoral neck fractures in pediatric patients with a femoral shaft
fracture is low (0.7%); therefore, routine preoperative CT is not recommended.14 If a
vascular injury is suspected, then CT angiography should be considered (pending

trauma/vascular surgery input). Stress fractures of the femoral shaft are rare; however,
MRI is the preferred imaging modality in such a scenario.
Management
A primary goal during the management of pediatric femur fractures is optimizing the patient-
specific risk/benefit profile en route to a healed fracture with acceptable radiographic
parameters (Table 2).
In general, treatment is age dependent, with considerable overlap existing between groups
(Table 3).
Patient weight, fracture pattern, and associated injuries may alter treatment decisions.
In pediatric patients, early definitive treatment has not been shown to alter pulmonary or
central nervous system (CNS) outcomes.
Management of femoral shaft fractures in patients with polytrauma (ie, damage control)
should incorporate standard orthopaedic trauma concepts. However, advantages such as the
ability to adequately resuscitate children and a multidisciplinary approach (with trauma
surgery, neurosurgery, etc.) should guide the timing and method of stabilization (Video 1).


Management
Younger patients with a femoral shaft fracture benefit from increased fracture stability
because of a thick periosteum, low-energy mechanisms of injury, fast healing, high
remodeling potential, and a lower burden of care. Therefore, in children younger than 4
or 5 years Pavlik harness management (young infants) or closed reduction during hip
spica casting (toddlers) is preferred. In preschoolers aged 4 to 5 years, the optimal
treatment option (ie, cast immobilization versus flexible intramedullary nailing) is a
subject of controversy.15 Patient age of 5 years is an inflection point, in which the
optimal treatment option for patients of that exact age is unclear and likely depends on
several factors (fracture pattern, mechanism, weight, social factors, etc.). With increasing
age, prolonged immobilization is less easily tolerated by the patient and/or family.16, 17
Therefore, a trend toward more functionally stable surgical stabilization of femoral
fractures has been increasing in children, with the use of flexible nails in those younger
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Femoral Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001058
12/31

than 5 years and the use of locked intramedullary nails in those younger than 11
years.18
Early versus delayed management of isolated pediatric femur fractures has not been
associated with altered clinical/functional outcomes. However, delayed management is
associated with longer intensive care and/or hospital length of stay.19 In pediatric
patients with a femoral shaft fracture and associated injuries after high-energy trauma,
damage control principles should be applied; however, children who are adequately
resuscitated usually can undergo definitive fixation early. A retrospective study of 387
pediatric trauma patients found similarly low rates of pulmonary complications after
early (<24 hours postinjury) versus late (≥24 hours postinjury) definitive treatment.20
With regard to closed head injuries, a small retrospective comparative cohort study
showed that delayed stabilization (≥48 hours) of an associated pediatric femur fracture
may increase hospital length of stay and the incidence of nonorthopaedic, non-CNS
outcomes, whereas early fixation (<48 hours) did not alter orthopaedic or CNS
outcomes.21 However, more than 50% of children in both of these studies were young
and were treated via hip spica casting and no patients in the early cohort in the CNS
study were treated via an intramedullary nail or open reduction and internal fixation.
This poses the question of whether surgeons should differentiate adult damage control
concepts from pediatric damage control concepts in stabilizing older, severely injured
children.
Open fractures should be managed according to standard principles. Patients with a
Gustilo and Anderson type I or type II fracture often can undergo definitive stabilization
after appropriate débridement. Patients with a type III fracture have the greatest risk of
deep infection and delayed union, making aggressive debridement essential. External
fixation often is used during interval debridements. The rates of delayed union and pin
tract infections are higher if external fixation is used as definitive fixation.22
Closed Management (Pavlik Harness and Hip Spica Casting)
Infants younger than 6 months can be treated in a Pavlik harness or a hip spica cast with
similar radiologic outcomes.

Moderate evidence supports early spica casting or traction with delayed spica casting for
children aged 6 months to 5 years with a diaphyseal femur fracture and less than 2 cm of
shortening.
Younger patients with stable fractures are candidates for a walking hip spica cast.</

Closed Management (Pavlik Harness and Hip Spica Casting)
A retrospective comparative study of 40 patients younger than 1 year with a femoral
shaft fracture (24 Pavlik harness versus 16 hip spica cast) reported similar healing times
(mean, 4 weeks) regardless of treatment; however, more skin complications were
reported in the hip spica group.23 The Pavlik harness group was younger and smaller.
Pain (and the family’s perception of pain) may be greater initially with Pavlik harness
management. Femoral nerve palsy is another complication associated with Pavlik
harness management; however, usually only moderate flexion is necessary to attain
appropriate alignment.
For children aged 6 months to 5 years who have a femoral fracture with less than 2 cm
of shortening, early hip spica casting is the most common treatment method. In previous
comparative studies, traction did not yield substantial benefits. Flynn et al24
demonstrated that patients with a low-energy fracture treated via an early walking hip
spica cast had similar clinical results but a lower burden of care compared with patients
treated via a traditional spica cast. Optimal management of fractures with greater than 2
cm of shortening and fractures in children aged 4 to 5 years are subjects of controversy.
Hip Spica Cast Technique
Proper hip spica cast application may minimize associated complications, such as interval
displacement necessitating revision, nerve palsy, and compartment syndrome.

Hip Spica Cast Technique
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM
AAOS | Pediatric Femoral Shaft Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001058
14/31

Hip spica casts without traction are most commonly used in patients with a fracture
from a low-energy mechanism. Compartment syndrome or peroneal nerve palsy may
develop if a preliminary short leg cast is used to distract the fracture before or during
proximal extension of a 90/90 cast into a hip spica cast25,26 (Figure 3; Resource 3).
Therefore, current recommendations indicate a preliminary long leg cast en route to a
45/45 hip spica cast, ensuring that the surgeon’s hands (rather than the cast) direct
fracture reduction. In addition, prospective studies demonstrated equivalent outcomes
with a single-leg spica compared with a double-leg spica. During casting, a
valgus/recurvatum mold usually is preferred, given the propensity of most fractures to
displace into varus and procurvatum.27 Pollak et al28 reported that 52% of high-energy
injuries required repeated manipulation (versus 8% of low-energy injuries, none of which
required traction). If skeletal traction is used, the distal femur is the preferred site to
avoid injury to the proximal tibial physis.29

Surgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001058
15/31

Most pediatric femoral shaft fractures in children aged 6 to 11 years are treated via flexible
intramedullary nails.
Higher rates of suboptimal outcomes with flexible nails in children aged 10 to 11 years or
older, weigh more than 49 kg, or have very proximal/distal or length-unstable fractures make
alternative techniques (eg, submuscular plate or locked, rigid intramedullary nail in children
older than 8 years) more appealing.
External fixation may be considered in any age group, and is most commonly used in patients
with severe soft-tissue injury, vascular compromise, or polytrauma.
Flexible Intramedullary Nails
Depending on the patient, flexible nails often are the most appealing option for extra-physeal
fixation.
Age younger than 10 years, weight less than 49 kg, and length-stable fractures are ideal patient
characteristics for optimal use of flexible intramedullary nails.
Proper surgical management of implants (eg, choice of titanium versus stainless steel,
obtaining 70% to 80% canal fill, avoiding nail prominence at entry sites) is important.

Flexible Intramedullary Nails
In patients aged 6 to 11 years with an ideal weight and fracture pattern, titanium flexible
intramedullary nails generally are considered excellent implants. Regardless, patients
who do not meet these criteria may still be successfully treated with the use of flexible
nails at the discretion of the surgeon. In younger patients with a less stable fracture
pattern, a supplementary hip spica cast can be applied until early callus formation is
visualized; however, whether a supplementary hip spica cast alters outcomes remains
unclear. In general, surgeons are taught to use two identical nails (diameter, type of
metal) in a C-C or C-S configuration, placed antegrade or retrograde (Video 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:36 PM

16/31

Video 2 Hosseinzadeh P: Flexible nailing of a femoral shaft fracture, from Hosseinzadeh
P, mod: A step-by-step guide to successful operative treatment of common fractures in
children: Indications, how to set up the room, position the patient, and do the
procedure. Presented at the Annual Meeting of the American Academy of Orthopaedic
Surgeons, Las Vegas, NV, March 12-16, 2019.
Symptomatic nail prominence at the site of entry was the most common minor
complication associated with the use of flexible intramedullary nails across multiple
series. To minimize this risk, extreme bending of the nail at the entry site should be
avoided. The surgeon also must determine how much prominence to accept during the
index procedure if subsequent removal is anticipated. Nail removal usually is performed
after union, typically 9 months postinjury. Retained implants may become unpredictably
symptomatic; waiting until after bony overgrowth occurs to remove implants may
complicate the procedure.30
Moroz et al31 retrospectively reviewed 234 femoral fractures managed with the use of
titanium elastic nails. Age (≥11 years) and weight (>49 kg) were the best predictors of
poor outcomes (primarily malunion with unresolved perioperative problems).
Specifically, outcomes were excellent in 71.9% of patients younger than 11 years versus
54.9% of patients aged 11 years or older (P = 0.003).31 In a series of 91 patients (94
fractures) treated with the use of titanium flexible nails, Ho et al32 reported a higher
complication rate in patients 10 years or older than in younger patients (34% versus 9%,

respectively; P < 0.01). Sink et al33 reviewed 39 fractures managed with the use of
titanium elastic nails and reported a higher rate of complications in length-unstable
fracture patterns.
None of the previous studies involved stainless steel elastic nails. In a biomechanical
study of stable fracture patterns, stainless steel nails demonstrated more resistance to
bending than titanium nails.34 Small comparative studies consisting of only stainless
steel flexible nails suggest their use may be acceptable in patients who weigh 100 lb or
more and have a length-unstable fracture.35,36
Sink et al33 also reported an increased rate of complications if the combined nail
diameter of titanium nails was less than 80% of the diameter of the intramedullary
canal.33 However, a study of 261 fractures managed with the use of stainless steel
flexible nails suggested that at least 70% canal fill may be adequate.36
Submuscular or Open Plating
In older/heavier children, children with a length-unstable fracture pattern, and children with a
very proximal/distal fracture, submuscular plating decreases the risk of malalignment
associated with flexible nails.
Submuscular plating also is useful in children older than 11 years with an intramedullary canal
that is too narrow for flexible nails or a rigid nail.

Submuscular or Open Plating
The optimal management of length-unstable or very proximal/distal femoral shaft
fractures in children older than 6 years remains a subject of controversy. However, many
believe that complication rates can be minimized in challenging pediatric femur fractures
by selecting the appropriate implant.9 Although high-quality evidence is limited,
submuscular plating of pediatric femur fractures is associated with lower rates of
malalignment (shortening or angulation), faster radiographic union, earlier weight

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001058
18/31

bearing, and an acceptably low complication profile when compared with flexible
intramedullary nailing.37,38
In children with a very proximal or distal femur fracture, fixation may be a challenge
without a rigid construct (Figures 4 and 5). During distal femur plate osteosynthesis, the
plate should be positioned at least 2 cm above the physis when possible to avoid
subsequent distal femoral valgus (reported in 30% of patients who were treated with
laterally placed plates39), and patients should undergo standing alignment radiographs
during follow-up. Occasionally, longer surgical times and increased intraoperative blood
loss are associated with the plating of femoral fractures; however, this also may reflect
more severe fracture patterns. The advantages of submuscular versus open plating also
are a subject of controversy. In theory, submuscular plating is a less invasive procedure
that provides slightly less reduction than open plating.40 Some studies recommend
appropriately timed plate removal before overgrowth to avoid late complications, such
as difficult removal, stress shielding, and prominent hardware.

Rigid, Locked Intramedullary Nails
Pediatric and adolescent lateral-entry, rigid, locked intramedullary nails are designed to enter
via the greater trochanteric apophysis and avoid vasculature that supplies the femoral head.
The greater trochanteric apophysis contributes to clinically meaningful growth until
approximately 8-9 years old.
Risks of rigid, locked intramedullary nail placement in children include femoral head
osteonecrosis (if nail entry or dissection is too medial), femoral neck narrowing, and coxa
valga.


Rigid, Locked Intramedullary Nails
Rigid, locked intramedullary nails have become the implant of choice in older (especially
older than 11 years) and heavier children, regardless of fracture pattern. A low (usually
asymptomatic) incidence of femoral neck narrowing and coxa valga has been reported
after nail placement through the greater trochanteric apophysis. The lowest age limit for
which this implant is appropriate remains unclear. At least one study included a patient
aged 7.3 years who had an acceptable outcome41 The authors concluded that clinically
meaningful changes in the proximal femur can be avoided in children aged 9 years or
older.41
Piriformis-entry rigid nails have been abandoned given the risk of femoral head
osteonecrosis.42 Instead, current implants are designed for far-lateral entry into the
greater trochanteric apophysis (Figure 6). No cases of osteonecrosis have been reported
using this far-lateral entry, and Keeler et al43 noted that more than 500 patients would
be required to demonstrate a 95% confidence interval of a risk of less than 1%. Nail
removal is not routinely performed, and some studies warn that the extensive,
unanticipated dissection required for implant removal may increase the risk iatrogenic
femoral head osteonecrosis. The incidence of symptomatic implants in younger patients
is unknown but may be related to longitudinal growth (Figure 7; Video 3).

A retrospective study of patients aged 8 to 17 years (mean age, 11.9 years) compared the
use of 102 lateral-entry, rigid intramedullary nails, 61 flexible nails, and 35 submuscular
plates for the management of pediatric diaphyseal femur fractures.44 The authors
concluded that rigid intramedullary nails were associated with the lowest rates of
malunion (2%) and hardware complications, flexible nails were associated with the
highest rates of malunion (22.4%) and symptomatic hardware (23.3%), and submuscular
plates were associated with the fastest time to radiographic union.44
External Fixation
External fixation is a viable option for the management of pediatric femur fractures in patients
of any age.
High rates of pin site infections and refracture explain why external fixation has been largely
replaced by alternative fixation methods.

Currently, external fixation is most appropriate in patients with extensive soft-tissue damage
or gross contamination (with or without an open fracture) that requires ongoing management,
patients with a severely unstable fracture, and patients with life-threatening injuries in whom
rapid stabilization is the best treatment option.

External Fixation
External fixation can restore length, provide rapid stabilization, and span a fracture site
without direct communication (preferred in patients with a severely open fracture or
gross contamination). Hybrid, circular, or monolateral external fixators have been
described. Pin site infections are the most common complication (up to 72.7% of
patients) but usually respond to pin care and oral antibiotic agents. Refracture after
fixator removal is reported in up to 21.6% of patients.45
Additional Outcomes and Complications
Given all the treatment options, the ultimate prognosis for patients with an isolated femur
fracture is good.
On average, leg-length discrepancy is approximately 1 cm and is clinically unimportant.
Angular deformity is better tolerated and/or remodels best in younger patients, in the sagittal
plane, and farther away from the knee.
Young patients may remodel or adapt to rotation deformity.

Additional Outcomes and Complications
On average, a 1-cm limb-length discrepancy can occur after the management of
pediatric femoral shaft fractures if less rigid fixation is used (eg, casting or flexible nails,
generally in patients aged 2 to 10 years). The discrepancy rarely requires subsequent
management, regardless of age. Shortening usually is fixation related, and lengthening
may result from overgrowth, fracture gapping, or malreduction of the femoral bow.46

Angular deformity generally is well tolerated. One study concluded that children younger
than 13 years can remodel up to 25° of varus/valgus in the middle third of the
diaphysis.47 Proximal third fractures often drift into varus. Patients treated via a spica
cast with fractures drifting into varus within the first few weeks of management may
respond to cast wedging. Malalignment (varus or valgus) close to the knee joint is poorly
tolerated.
Techniques to avoid malrotation should be applied during the index procedure. For
example, during hip spica casting, the contralateral limb can be used to estimate
appropriate limb rotation. Similarly, various techniques have been developed (and
described mostly in the adult literature) to prevent malrotation during rigid
intramedullary nailing on a fracture table.
